title: The Calculator Riot of 1986 and the Modern Myth of the “Dumb” AI Teacher
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele opens with the 1986 teacher protests against calculators in the classroom and argues that today's resistance to AI in teachers' workflows repeats the same mistake. He points out that the system found an equilibrium by separating conceptual mastery from automation, and that students already use AI whatever schools decide. He then shows how he uses a customised Gemini setup for planning: interactive HTML lessons instead of slides, atomised maths worksheets built to cognitive load principles, calibrated sequences of examples and non-examples drawn from variation theory, code-built Do Nows, and AI as an editor of his own drafted communications. His caveat is that AI amplifies expertise rather than replacing it, since weak pedagogical knowledge produces weak prompts and generic resources. The case is practical and first-person, aimed squarely at teachers.
points: The 1986 calculator protests are a historical parallel: bans delayed guided adoption, and curricula eventually separated fluency from automation.
Because students already use AI, refusing to engage leaves teachers less able to guide how it is used.
He replaces slide decks with Gemini-generated interactive web pages, and generates atomised worksheets, example and non-example sequences, and Do Nows tailored to exact learning intentions.
He keeps the thinking and structure his own and uses AI as an editor for parent emails and references, not a ghostwriter.
AI only yields useful output if the teacher already understands cognitive load, misconceptions and explicit instruction.
quotes: Far from making students “dumber,” the calculator became a tool to bypass low-level cognitive bottlenecks once the underlying foundation was secure.

It ignores a simple, unyielding truth: your students are already using it. Whether we like it or not, they are utilising AI to structure their homework, draft essays, and act as personalised out-of-school tutors.
Instead, I prompt Gemini to generate clean, lightweight, interactive single-page web applications.

According to Cognitive Load Theory, working memory is strictly limited. To prevent overload, we must break a complex routine down into its constituent “atoms” and ensure students achieve absolute fluency in Atoms 1, 2, and 3 before chaining them into a full process.
The AI handles the combinatorial heavy lifting, allowing me to review, refine, and select the sequence that will best expose student misconceptions during the “I do / We do” phase of the lesson.

The AI acts not as a ghostwriter, but as an editor. It polishes the language, cleans up syntax errors, and ensures that my communication is immaculate and professional, saving hours of staring at a blank screen.

If you do not understand cognitive load theory, if you cannot spot a subtle mathematical misconception, and if you don’t understand the nuance of explicit instruction, you cannot write a prompt that yields anything useful. The machine will simply output generic, shallow resources.
